position: BUILD — but build the origin, not the edge. Mehfilbox should own ingest (tusd), transcoding (FFmpeg ladder + HLS packaging + posters + seek VTT), object storage (Backblaze B2), signed-URL minting and per-object usage metering, and should keep buying delivery from Bunny as a dumb CDN pull zone. That is the only version of 'build our own' that survives its own cost model: it removes the three Bunny constraints that are actively costing money and correctness today (library-wide keep-originals, unenforceable 4K minutes, watch-time-estimated billing) while not picking a fight over India-PoP delivery, which Bunny wins at $0.030/GB and nobody self-serve beats. The full-stack version — own CDN too — is not defensible before roughly 1,000 weddings/month and I will not argue for it. The 'own IP for grants' argument is worth zero and I concede it outright.
summary: The honest case for building is not a cheaper bill. Infrastructure-only, at the SCALE-PLAN ladder-only storage profile, the recommended stack costs about Rs 48,900/month at 60 weddings/month against Bunny's Rs 45,207 — a Rs 3,700 loss. The case turns on the storage profile actually in production: lib/video/bunny.ts:198-201 says the library keeps originals with MP4 fallback on, and docs/PRICING.md Section 5 prices renditions at roughly 30 percent on top of originals, so real stored volume is about 3.5x the modelled ladder. At that profile the same 60 weddings cost Bunny about Rs 99,700/month and cost the self-hosted stack about Rs 86,800 — and with per-plan retention, which Bunny structurally cannot do because keep-originals is one library-wide toggle for all three plans, about Rs 75,000. That is a Rs 25,000/month infra swing at the scale the six-month plan actually targets, roughly an order of magnitude earlier than cost.json's R2-plus-Cloudflare stack crosses, and it exists only because you own the origin. Three correctness wins come free with it and cannot be bought from Bunny at any price: real delivered bytes per catalogue from CDN logs instead of watch_seconds times a 2.15 GB/hour placeholder (lib/video/bunny.ts:234-262, lib/entitlements.ts:131 — you are metering customer credits off an assumption today); a per-title encoding ladder, which is the only way the Cinema plan's 4K allowance becomes enforceable at all, since resolutions are a Bunny library setting and nothing in lib/, app/ or components/ sets enabledResolutions or references 2160/1440 anywhere; and a webhook that is your own queue rather than an account-key-gated dashboard field this repository cannot read, verify or change, which already broke the second-pass go-live (map-media-infra.md Section 7.4, docs/GO-LIVE.md:213-244). Timing is the fourth argument and the sharpest: the product promises the wedding survives the studio, so the archive only ever grows and migration egress grows with it. Moving today's roughly 3,800 GB out of Bunny at Asia rates costs about Rs 11,000; the same move at 300 weddings/month moves 114 TB and costs about Rs 3.3 lakh. If this is ever going to happen, it is about 30x cheaper now than at the scale where the spreadsheet finally agrees. What defeats all of this is people. Rs 70,000/month of ops headcount at 60 weddings is larger than the entire infra saving, and no scenario in cost.json breaks even once headcount is counted. So the build is justified if and only if Sandeep believes he is hiring an SRE anyway — which the Supabase, Vercel, six-cron and wedding-night on-call surface says he is, somewhere between 60 and 300 weddings — and wants that person's first project to be the one that also fixes the metering and the retention policy. If the honest answer is 'no SRE for two years', the numbers say stay on Bunny and I would not overrule them.
architecture: Own origin, borrowed edge. Every Bunny feature in map-media-infra.md Section 3 replaced one for one, behind the existing seam. (1) INGEST: tusd (github.com/tus/tusd, MIT) with the S3 multipart backend on one Hetzner CCX23/CCX33, fronted by a pre-signed creation ticket with the same shape as lib/video/bunny.ts:74-93 — sha256(secret + expiry + assetId) validated server-side, key never in the browser. TUS is a published protocol, not a Bunny API, so components/admin/UploadManager.tsx:67-83 (resume from the server-acked offset) and its 409/423 retry classification at :145-155 carry over byte-for-byte; this is the single riskiest file in the repo per CLAUDE.md and it is the part that does not change. (2) TRANSCODE: FFmpeg workers, x264 on CPU boxes to 300 weddings/month, NVENC on a Hetzner GEX44 (RTX 4000 SFF Ada) or an AWS g4dn.xlarge in Mumbai above that. One job emits the whole contract getStatus already promises: the 360/480/720/1080 fMP4 HLS ladder (plus 2160 only for Cinema titles, decided per title from lib/entitlements), thumbnail_1..3.jpg poster candidates, and seek/seek.vtt — exactly the file names lib/video/bunny.ts:130-131,181-189 hands the player, so the player, the poster route and the customizer preview are untouched. (3) QUEUE: the existing Postgres job runner, lib/jobs/run.ts:18-46, plus a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED claim and the retry/stall semantics app/api/cron/reconcile/route.ts already implements. No new infrastructure line, no Redis, no SQS. (4) STORAGE: Backblaze B2 at $6.95/TB-month, chosen over R2 ($0.015/GB) because R2 is 1.5x Bunny's own storage price and would lose the argument outright; B2 egress to Bunny is free under the Bandwidth Alliance, which is what makes the borrowed-edge design cost nothing extra. Layout mirrors lib/photos/index.ts:35-42: v/<assetId>/<rendition>/... and v/<assetId>/original. Retention is a per-title column driven by the catalogue's plan — originals kept for Keep and Cinema, dropped after 30 days for Deliver — which is the single largest cost lever in the model and the one Bunny cannot offer. (5) DELIVERY: a Bunny CDN pull zone in front of the B2 origin, 119 PoPs, India included, at the same $0.030/GB already being paid. This deliberately does not move; cost.json's own note says Cloudflare's self-serve terms restrict video through the CDN to Stream or Enterprise, and CloudFront India at $0.109/GB is 3.6x Bunny. (6) SIGNED URLS: Bunny pull-zone token authentication uses the same base64url(sha256(key + path + expires)) construction already implemented at lib/video/bunny.ts:137-147, still signing the DIRECTORY not the manifest — the child-playlist 403 trap is HLS behaviour, not a vendor quirk, and pnpm verify:playback keeps proving it. Zero change to getPlaybackToken or getAssetUrl. (7) WEBHOOK: workers POST to /api/webhooks/transcode with HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body, same construction as lib/video/bunny.ts:264-305, keyed by an env secret lib/env.ts owns. The handler already treats the payload as 'something changed, go ask getStatus', so it is unchanged and stays idempotent — and preflight.ts can finally assert the webhook target, which it cannot do against Bunny (map Section 7.4). (8) METERING: getUsage reads B2/CDN log-derived per-object bytes, so Usage.deliveredGb becomes measured and Usage.watchSeconds stays measured beside it — the deliberate separation lib/video/provider.ts already documents finally has real numbers on both sides. (9) PHOTOS: already only PUT/GET against a storage zone behind a pull zone (lib/photos/bunny.ts:1-68) and scripts/repoint-photo-cdn.ts already exists to move them; this is a re-point, not a rewrite. (10) OPS: extend app/api/cron/synthetic/route.ts past the token to actually fetch one segment — today it deliberately stops short so a Bunny edge hiccup does not page you for Bunny's outage; when the origin is yours, being paged is the correct behaviour. Grafana Cloud free tier plus Better Stack uptime at $29. Everything lands behind lib/video/provider.ts's seven methods, whose own docstring calls the Bunny driver a default and not a lock-in; the fake driver and the whole CI suite (VIDEO_DRIVER=fake) never notice.
benefits: Per-plan retention, which Bunny structurally forbids. Keep-originals and MP4 fallback are ONE library-wide setting and they are ON in production (lib/video/bunny.ts:198-201) — so every Deliver wedding is storing an untouched multi-gigabyte original the plan never promised, alongside its ladder. docs/PRICING.md Section 5 prices this at roughly 30 percent of renditions on top of originals, i.e. about 3.5x the ladder-only volume cost.json models. Owning the origin makes retention a per-title column: originals for Keep and Cinema, ladder-only for Deliver after 30 days. At 60 weddings/month that is roughly Rs 25,000/month against Bunny's real bill — larger than the entire modelled infra delta, and unavailable at any price from Bunny because turning the toggle off there would break the 'originals downloadable untouched' promise for Keep and Cinema at the same time.

Delivered gigabytes become measured instead of assumed. lib/video/bunny.ts:234-262 derives deliveredGb from watchTimeChart times GB_PER_HOUR.standard = 2.15, and lib/entitlements.ts:119-131 flags that constant as an estimate pending N-24a. Bunny reports bandwidth only per pull zone — the whole library — so per-catalogue delivery cannot be measured there, ever. An own origin yields real bytes per object from CDN logs. This is a commerce-correctness fix, not a cost fix: usage_rollup.delivered_gb feeds credit accounting and the 300 GB over-delivery alert (app/api/cron/usage/route.ts), and today both are running off a placeholder.

The 4K allowance becomes enforceable. grep across lib/, app/ and components/ finds no reference to 2160, 1440, enabledResolutions or premium anywhere — because resolutions are a Bunny LIBRARY setting, not a per-video one. The Cinema plan's premium-encoding allowance is therefore an unmetered, unbounded cost line: nothing in the product can stop a Deliver customer's upload from being encoded at 4K and billed at $0.150/min. An own encoder picks the ladder per title from the catalogue's entitlements at job submission, and removes the premium line entirely — Rs 1,436/month at 10 weddings rising to Rs 1.44 lakh at 1,000 (cost.json).

The webhook stops being an out-of-band setting nobody can verify. The Bunny webhook URL is an account-key-gated dashboard field this repository deliberately never holds the key for (docs/DEPLOYMENT.md:58-68); scripts/preflight.ts:102-284 checks every other Bunny setting and cannot check this one. It already caused a real incident at the second-pass go-live, and docs/GO-LIVE.md:213-244 names the failure mode precisely — uploads succeed, encoding finishes, titles simply never leave processing, and the webhook answers 200 from superseded code the whole time. When the worker is yours, the callback target is an env var lib/env.ts validates and preflight asserts.

Migration cost is at its lifetime minimum right now. The product's own guarantee is that the wedding survives the studio, so the archive is append-only with 12-month-plus retention. Egressing the current roughly 3,800 GB out of Bunny at Asia rates is about $114, roughly Rs 11,000. The identical decision at 300 weddings/month moves 114 TB and costs about Rs 3.3 lakh in egress before a single engineer-hour. The option is about 30x cheaper today than at the scale where the spreadsheet finally agrees with it, and it decays monotonically.

Vendor concentration collapses from four risks to one. Today Bunny holds the masters, the transcode, the CDN, the signed-URL authority and the originals that back the download promise. A billing dispute, an account suspension or a regional policy change takes the entire product down at once, and lib/downloads.ts's 'original' label becomes a lie in the same instant. Under the proposed split, losing Bunny costs a CDN pull zone — a DNS change and a new pull zone in front of the same B2 origin, hours not months.

Real cache and first-play control. Bunny Stream's storage is in Singapore (lib/photos/bunny.ts:16-17 — Bunny has no India origin, Mumbai is 'planned'). The Phase 0 definition of done is a film starting in under 1.5 seconds on 4G, and a private wedding catalogue with 300 guests spread over days is mostly cache-MISS traffic, not viral traffic. An origin you place (or a warm-on-publish job that pre-pulls the first segments of every film into the India PoPs at Publish time) is something you can only build when the origin is yours.

Encoding policy becomes a product surface rather than a vendor default: per-title bitrate ladders tuned for the 2.15 GB/hour figure the pricing model depends on, AV1 or HEVC for the archive tier later, and an honest measured replacement for N-24a's placeholder as a by-product of running the encoder.
costs_and_losses: Infrastructure, honestly: at the ladder-only profile cost.json models, the recommended stack is Rs 48,900/month at 60 weddings/month against Bunny's Rs 45,207 — it LOSES by about Rs 3,700. It wins only against the storage profile actually in production (originals kept): roughly Rs 86,800 against Bunny's roughly Rs 99,700, falling to roughly Rs 75,000 with per-plan retention. Composition at 60/month: B2 storage $158 ladder-only or $555 with originals, 2x CCX33 encoders plus 1x CCX33 tusd ingest EUR 145.50 (about Rs 16,100), Bunny pull-zone delivery 5,148 GB at $0.030 = $154, monitoring $29.

People, which decide it and which I am not going to hide behind. cost.json's headcount ladder — Rs 35,000/month at 10 weddings, Rs 70,000 at 60, Rs 2 lakh at 300, Rs 4 lakh at 1,000 — exceeds the entire Bunny bill until about 300 weddings/month and exceeds the infra saving at every scale tested. Including people there is NO breakeven anywhere in the modelled range, and the curves only touch near 1,000 weddings/month under the most aggressive stack. Today's Bunny path carries effectively zero dedicated ops headcount.

Build: roughly 8-12 engineer-weeks for the core pipeline (cost.json), which I have grossed up to 5 engineer-months over 4 calendar months once migration, a dual-run period, the runbook and the ops hardening are counted — about Rs 6-9 lakh at Indian contract rates, plus EUR 79 per GPU box setup. Those are founder-months or contractor-rupees not spent on N-20 (payment gateway), the theme store, or direct-to-client onboarding.

Free standard encoding is given up. Bunny charges nothing for the whole sub-1080p ladder. At 10 weddings/month a two-box pipeline runs at roughly 14 percent utilisation and its fixed floor alone exceeds the entire Bunny bill (Rs 19,971 vs Rs 7,534 in cost.json's R2 variant). Below about 40 weddings/month this decision is straightforwardly wrong.

Encoding quality regresses before it improves. Bunny's ladder is tuned; a first x264 ladder will be worse per delivered byte, which shows up as both a worse first-play and a higher delivery bill, until somebody spends real time on it. Nothing in this repo has ever measured encode quality.

Wedding-night blast radius moves onto us. app/api/cron/synthetic/route.ts:29-31 deliberately stops at the token rather than fetching a manifest, with the stated reasoning that a Bunny edge hiccup must not page us for Bunny's outage. Building inverts that on purpose: a stuck encode at 11pm on a Saturday becomes a phone call, and Indian weddings cluster Nov-Feb, so peak is far above the monthly average the boxes are sized on.

A one-way-ish migration of live customer data. Every original must be egressed out of Bunny, re-encoded (or its ladder copied), and every titles.provider_id re-pointed, while guests are watching. Cheap now; it is still the class of operation where a bug loses somebody's wedding.

Hardware supply risk that is already real: the Hetzner GEX44 the GPU tier depends on was listed out of stock as of July 2026, and the AWS g4dn.xlarge Mumbai fallback at $0.577/hour has roughly half the NVENC throughput. CPU-only 4K runs at about 0.3x real time, which makes a 60-minute Cinema film a multi-hour job.
risks: The Rs 25,000/month storage argument depends entirely on the keep-originals reading being correct, and a much cheaper experiment tests it first: turn keep-originals off on the Bunny library and measure. That recovers most of the storage saving for zero engineer-months — at the cost of the 'originals downloadable untouched' promise for Keep and Cinema, which is exactly the trade-off the build avoids. If Sandeep is willing to drop that promise, the strongest financial leg of this case disappears.

The people cost is not optional and is the thing that kills the spreadsheet. If the SRE is not hired anyway for Supabase, Vercel, the six crons and wedding-night on-call, this build converts a zero-headcount dependency into a permanent one, and every scenario in cost.json says that is a losing trade.

Bunny may respond with a committed contract. docs/SCALE-PLAN.md Section 5 already says to negotiate past 10 TB/month; any discount pushes the crossing further out and could erase the storage advantage at exactly the scale where the build is meant to pay off.

Keeping Bunny as the pull zone means the delivery dependency — the largest marginal line at $2.57 per wedding — is not actually removed. The vendor-independence claim is partial: it is an origin migration, not an exit.

The TUS resume path is the place CLAUDE.md and doc 13 Section 7 both say the schedule slips (components/admin/UploadManager.tsx:67-83). tusd implements the same protocol, but the S3 multipart backend's offset acknowledgement semantics under a mid-upload network drop are the exact behaviour scripts/verify-upload-resume.ts exists to test, and it must pass against tusd before anything ships.

Cross-border origin latency on cold cache. Neither B2 (US/EU) nor Hetzner (EU) has an Indian region, so a cache-miss first play may be SLOWER than Bunny's Singapore origin until a warm-on-publish job exists. That directly threatens the Phase 0 definition of done and must be measured, not assumed.

Seasonality: boxes sized at 1.3x the monthly average will be undersized in the Nov-Feb cluster, and a queue backlog during peak season is visible to studios as 'my films are still processing' on the worst possible week.
Founder-attention risk. research-fit.json's action 5 says plainly: do not build this as part of the fundraising motion. Running both at once is how neither finishes.
what_it_does_not_fix: It does not make the bill cheaper at current scale. At 10 weddings/month self-hosting is 2.6x dearer on infrastructure alone and 7.3x dearer including the cheapest honest ops cover.

It does not help with grants, and this must not be claimed. SISFS Guidelines Section 8.1.3 states the seed fund 'shall strictly not be used by startups for creation of any facilities' — an in-house pipeline is precisely that. The Novelty criterion (Section 7.2.v) scores 'USP of the technology, associated IP', and transcoding is commodity engineering that Bunny gives away free; a reviewer who knows the space will read 'we built our own FFmpeg pipeline' as a cost centre, not IP. DPIIT recognition is free, self-certified, and does not score architecture at all (startupindia.gov.in, 14 Sep 2026). The defensible novelty already exists elsewhere in the product — 10-15-hour multi-function wedding capacity no competitor's plan holds, a browsable catalogue instead of a password-gated grid, the archive-not-delete guarantee — and none of it depends on who encodes the video. The own-IP-for-grants argument is worth zero and I am not going to pretend otherwise.

It does not remove the Bunny dependency, by design: delivery stays on Bunny's pull zone because that is the one line no self-serve alternative beats for India (CloudFront India is 3.6x; Cloudflare's own policy page restricts video via CDN to Stream or Enterprise on self-serve plans).

It does not fix the highest-severity defect on this subsystem map, which has nothing to do with Bunny: the Supabase repository driver ignores the live_at publish gate for both titles and photographs (lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1390-1396,1625-1631), so guests can see unpublished content in production. That is a one-line-per-query fix and it outranks every word of this document.

It does not fix the sequential catalogue-delete cleanup loop (up to 195 sequential provider round-trips, app/api/admin/catalogues/[id]/route.ts:159-174), the silently-skipped photo rendition PUT failures (lib/photos/bunny.ts:37-56), or the fact that photo deletes remove only the master rendition. Those are ours already.

It does not replace N-24a. The 2.15 GB/hour placeholder is replaced by measurement only if someone actually wires the log pipeline and reads it; owning the origin makes the measurement possible, not automatic.
It does nothing for the Go/Java port question, the theme store, or direct-to-client onboarding, and it competes with all three for the same founder-hours.
triggers_to_revisit: Sustained volume above roughly 40-60 weddings/month AND a decision to hire an SRE for reasons that exist independently of this project. Below that, the fixed floor of a two-box pipeline exceeds the whole Bunny bill; without the second condition, the headcount line eats every saving.

A measurement of actual stored gigabytes per wedding on the live Bunny library. If real storage is close to the 31.7 GB ladder-only figure, the central financial argument here is wrong and the answer is stay on Bunny. If it is 100-130 GB as docs/PRICING.md Section 5 implies, build.

A decision that the 'originals downloadable untouched' promise is load-bearing for Keep and Cinema. If it is, Bunny cannot offer per-plan retention and the build is the only way to get it. If it is not, turn keep-originals off on Bunny first and re-run these numbers — that experiment costs one afternoon.

The first month where premium 4K encoding minutes exceed roughly Rs 25,000, or the first customer dispute over a delivered-gigabyte figure that turns out to be watch_seconds times 2.15. Either one converts an architectural argument into a commercial one.

Bunny changing Asia-Oceania delivery pricing, imposing account limits on a single library's size, or opening a Mumbai storage region (currently 'planned'). The last of those materially weakens the origin-latency argument for building.

A second, non-wedding use of the pipeline — corporate events, a partner white-label, a media customer — which is the only thing that would make an owned pipeline a product rather than a cost centre, and the only framing under which a grant reviewer's Novelty criterion would engage with it at all.
Any month where the reconcile cron has to settle more than a handful of titles, or the webhook drifts again after a domain change. Recurrence turns a vendor inconvenience into a reliability case.

Approaching 300 weddings/month, where the Vercel function-invocation ceiling (docs/SCALE-PLAN.md Section 3) forces an architecture conversation anyway and the ops headcount is being paid regardless — the cheapest moment to fold this in.
migration_path: 0. Before anything: fix the live_at publish-gate bug in the Supabase driver, and run the free experiment — read the Bunny library's real stored bytes and decide whether keep-originals is deliberate. If the storage profile turns out to be ladder-only, stop here; the financial case does not exist and staying on Bunny is correct.

1. Contract freeze (about 1 week). Write the acceptance suite against lib/video/provider.ts's seven methods with no Bunny types in sight — tests that any driver must pass: directory-scoped token authorises a child playlist, a file-scoped one does not; posterCandidates are thumbnail_1..3.jpg; the webhook verifier rejects a re-serialised body. This is the artefact that makes the rest reversible, and it is worth writing even if the build is cancelled.

2. Ingest first, alone (about 3 weeks). Stand up tusd with the S3 multipart backend against B2 and run scripts/verify-upload-resume.ts against it — a real production build, a real browser, a real mid-transfer network drop, asserting the percentage never regresses. If tusd cannot pass that test, stop the project here; it is the cheapest possible place to fail.

3. Encoder in shadow mode (about 4 weeks). FFmpeg workers on one CCX33, fed by the existing lib/jobs/run.ts queue, transcoding a COPY of every new upload while Bunny stays authoritative. Compare ladder output, storage footprint, poster frames and seek VTT against Bunny's for the same sources. Nothing user-facing changes; the only cost is one box.

4. SelfHostedVideoProvider behind the seam (about 3 weeks). Implement all seven methods, sign the B2-backed Bunny pull zone with the existing base64url(sha256(...)) construction, add /api/webhooks/transcode with the same HMAC shape, teach scripts/preflight.ts to assert the webhook target — the check that is impossible against Bunny — and run the whole suite on VIDEO_DRIVER=selfhosted.

5. Prove it live on the demo catalogue (about 1 week). Point DEMO_CATALOGUE_SLUG at the new provider, run pnpm verify:playback end to end (signed manifest, signed CHILD playlist, signed poster, unsigned 403 on all three, a real hls.js player reaching decoded frames), and extend app/api/cron/synthetic/route.ts to fetch a real segment now that the origin is ours. Measure first-play on an actual 4G handset in India against the 1.5-second Phase 0 bar. If it misses, fix the warm-on-publish job before proceeding — this is the gate that protects the definition of done.

6. New weddings only, for one full month (about 4 weeks elapsed, low effort). Route new catalogues to the new provider per-org; existing weddings stay on Bunny. Both drivers live behind the same seam, so a single env flip reverts any studio. Watch reconcile, job_runs and the delivered-bytes figures against the old estimate — the first real read of how wrong 2.15 GB/hour was.

7. Backfill the archive (about 2 weeks, mostly waiting). Egress every original out of Bunny (about Rs 11,000 today), re-encode into the new ladder with per-plan retention applied, re-point titles.provider_id in batches with verification per title, and keep the Bunny library intact and paid for 60 days as the rollback. Photos move by re-pointing the pull zone with the existing scripts/repoint-photo-cdn.ts.

8. Decommission and write the runbook (about 1 week). Delete the Bunny Stream library only after 60 clean days. Document the on-call path for a stuck encode on a Saturday night, because that is the cost this whole decision actually buys, and nobody should discover it during a wedding.
